blocks.text: What is πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς ἐν καρτάλλῳ [perdix thēreutēs en kartallō], the hunter partridge in a cage, Sirach. XI, 31. var. 37.

Having dealt with the spurious partridge, we shall say a little about the genuine one, with reference to the well-known passage of Sirach, Eccles. XI, 31. var. 37: Πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς ἐν καρτάλλῳ, οὕτως καρδία ὑπερηφάνου, καὶ ὡς ὁ κατάσκοπος ἐπιβλέπει πτῶσιν [Perdix thēreutēs en kartallō, houtōs kardia hyperēphanou, kai hōs ho kataskopos epiblepei ptōsin]; Like a hunter partridge in a cage, so is the heart of the proud man, who like a spy watches for a fall. The sense is that a proud man, when another has been driven to ruin, exults over him in the same way as the hunter partridge in a cage exults over the birds of its own kind that it has led into the snare. For there πέρδιξ θηρευτὴς [perdix thēreutēs] is a tame partridge, which by its arts lures wild partridges into the cage or the snares. Aristotle, History book 9, ch. 8: Καὶ τῶν περδίκων δ᾽ οἱ τιθασσοὶ τοὺς ἀγρίους πέρδικας ὀχεύουσι, καὶ ἐπικορίζουσι [kai tōn perdikōn d᾽ hoi tithassoi tous agrious perdikas ocheuousi, kai epikorizousi] (read ἐπικοῤῥίζουσι [epikorrizousi]) καὶ ὑβρίζουσιν. Ἐπὶ δὲ τὸν θηρευτὴν πέρδικα ὠθεῖται τῶν ἀγρίων ὁ ἡγεμὼν, ἀντιάσας ὡς μαχούμενος, τούτου δ᾽ ἁλόντος ἐν ταῖς πηκταῖς, πάλιν προσέρχεται ἄλλος, ἀντιάσας τὸν αὐτὸν τρόπον [kai hybrizousin. Epi de ton thēreutēn perdika ōtheitai tōn agriōn ho hēgemōn, antiasas hōs machoumenos, toutou d᾽ halontos en tais pēktais, palin proserchetai allos, antiasas ton auton tropon]. Tame partridges also tread the wild partridges, and beat them, and treat them with insult. And the leader of the wild ones rushes at the hunter partridge, advancing against it as if to fight. When he has been caught in the wicker cage, another in turn comes forward against it in the same way. You see in both places τὸν θηρευτὴν πέρ- [col. 90] δικα [ton thēreutēn perdika], the hunter partridge, and the wicker cage. For that is properly κάρταλλος [kartallos] in Sirach, as αἱ πήκται [hai pēktai] is in the Philosopher. Hesychius: Κάρταλον [Kartalon] (read Κάρταλλον [Kartallon]): τὸ πλεκτὸν ἀγγεῖον [to plekton angeion] (I would prefer πηκτὸν [pēkton], as in Aristotle) ἐν τοῖς ὀψαρτυτικοῖς κλωβός [en tois opsartytikois klōbos]. Quite correctly. For a cage of this kind is also called κλωβὸς [klōbos], as in Hebrew כלוב club, and in Syriac ܩܠܘܒܝܐ klubja. Thus Ierem. V, 27: ככלוב מלא עוף, like a cluub (cage) teeming with birds. Here the Syriac has ܐܝܟ ܩܠܘܒܝܐ, like a klubja (although the Greeks have ὡς παγὶς ἐφεσταμένη [hōs pagis ephestamenē], and the Arabic مثل فخ منصوب [mithl fakhkh manṣūb] [II, 646] ܡܨܝܕܬܐ like a set snare, and Jerome like a trap). For the subject is a cage into which birds are lured, as is clear from the whole context. For the verse immediately preceding reads: For among my people are found those who lie in wait like fowlers, setting snares to catch men. And this verse itself: Like a club teeming with birds, so their houses are full of deceit, that is, of things gained and acquired by deceit. Thus, a point that has escaped the lexicographers: just as כלוב club occurs in the Hebrew text of Jeremiah, so also in Greek writers κλουβὸς [kloubos] or κλωβὸς [klōbos] occurs elsewhere too, either for this deceitful cage or for any cage at all. Oppian in the Ixeutica [III, 14.], on the aegithus: It is caught κλωβῷ [klōbō], in a cage, in which another bird, caught earlier, is shut up to lure it by its voice. An old poet in Suidas, under Ἀμφιῤῥῶγας [Amphirrhōgas]: Κλωβοὺς τ᾽ ἀμφιῤῥῶγας [Klōbous t᾽ amphirrhōgas], cages broken on all sides. Philostorgius book 10, ch. 11 (in my manuscript, which is often more correct than the printed copy), on the Egyptian dwarf: Ὁ δὲ Αἰγύπτιος οὕτω κατεβραχύνετο, ὥστε μηδ᾽ ἀχαρίστως τοὺς ἐν τοῖς κλουβοῖς πέρδικας ἐκμιμεῖσθαι, καὶ συναθύρειν αὐτῷ πρὸς ἔριν ἐκείνους [Ho de Aigyptios houtō katebrachyneto, hōste mēd᾽ acharistōs tous en tois kloubois perdikas ekmimeisthai, kai synathyrein autō pros erin ekeinous]; The Egyptian was so stunted that he imitated, not unpleasingly, the partridges shut up in clubs (or cages), which themselves contended with him in play. And Nicephorus, book 12, ch. 37, says that the same man was παραπλήσιον πέρδικι, καὶ μὴ ἀχάριστον ἐν κλωβῷ τὴν ἐκείνου προσομιλίαν [paraplēsion perdiki, kai mē acharislon en klōbō tēn ekeinou prosomilian]. And Cedrenus, Paris edition, p. 592 B: Ζῶον ἦν τι πτῆνον ἐν κλωβῷ κατὰ τὰ βασίλεια αἰωρούμενον [Zōon ēn ti ptēnon en klōbō kata ta basileia aiōroumenon]. There was a certain bird in the palace, hung up in a clobus (that is, a cage). The Glosses of Philoxenus: Κλωβὸς [Klōbos], cavea [cage]. Therefore a very learned man wishes in vain to change κλουβοῖς [klouhois] in Philostorgius to κλοιοῖς [kloiois] or κλυβοῖς [klybois]. And the translator of Nicephorus rendered the words ἐν κλωβῷ [en klōbō] quite absurdly: In a globe, namely of men. The Talmudists, in the tractate Kilaim, call a cage for catching birds פלצור paltsur, and the Romans transenna. Plautus in the Bacchides, act 4, the scene Nimio:
Now this thrush is going for the worm from the trap. He will hang there nicely today, so well have I set the snare.
And in the Persa, act 4, the scene Cui homini:
Today I shall lead this man into the trap with clever tricks.
And in the Rudens, act 4, the scene Quam mox:
O Gripus, Gripus, in men's lifetime there come to be very many traps, in which they are caught by tricks ^{(1)}.
